summary: Explains what Mobile IP is meant for, summarizes its key features, and shows that it satisfied the requirements for advancing to Proposed Standard. It is an applicability statement accompanying the main Mobile IP specification.

eli5.summary: This is a note saying what a tool is good for and proving it passed the tests it needed to pass.

subtitle: A short note on what Mobile IP is good for, and proof that it was ready to become a Proposed Standard.

tldr.problem: Before the Mobile IP specification could advance to Proposed Standard, the working group had to show where the protocol applies and that it met the advancement requirements of RFC 1264.
tldr.mechanism: The statement summarizes how Mobile IP tunnels packets from a home agent to a care-of address, says where it fits and where it does not, and reports an interoperability test of several implementations.
tldr.outcome: The co-chairs concluded the requirements were satisfied: a stable specification, a MIB, a security architecture in line with IAB principles, and interoperable independent implementations.

today: RFC 2005 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is an applicability statement for the Mobile IP specification in RFC 2002.

sections.title: How Mobile IP Works in Brief
sections.content:
Mobile IP lets a node change its point of attachment to the Internet without changing its IP address, so transport and higher-layer connections keep working while it moves. No host-specific routes need to be spread through the Internet routing fabric.

Packets for a mobile node go first to its home network. There the home agent intercepts them and tunnels them to the node's most recently reported care-of address. At the end of the tunnel the inner packet is unwrapped and delivered. Packets sent by the mobile node use standard IP routing.

The protocol defines an authenticated registration procedure, an extension to ICMP Router Discovery (RFC 1256) for finding home and foreign agents, and the routing rules, including one mandatory tunneling mechanism and several optional ones. The main specification is RFC 2002.
sections.eli5: Imagine your mail always goes to your old house, and someone there forwards it to wherever you are staying now. You keep one home address, no matter where you travel.

sections.title: Where Mobile IP Fits
sections.content:
Mobile IP is meant for mobility across changes of IP subnet, whether the move is between similar media (one Ethernet segment to another) or different ones (Ethernet to a wireless LAN). The statement calls this the "macro" mobility problem.

It is less well suited to "micro" mobility, such as handoff among wireless transceivers that each cover a very small area. There, link-layer handoff might converge faster with less overhead.

Without route optimization, the home agent can become a load point when it serves many mobile nodes. Extra home agents can be added, and mobile nodes can discover them dynamically. Mobile IP also does not try to solve IP address renumbering: home addresses are assigned much like long-term addresses of stationary hosts.
sections.eli5: It works well for moving between buildings, but not for tiny steps like walking from one room to the next, where a simpler local trick is faster.

sections.title: Security of Registration
sections.content:
Mobile IP requires cryptographically strong authentication for all registration messages between a mobile node and its home agent. Replay protection uses either timestamps or nonces. Every implementation must support at least keyed MD5 authentication with manual key distribution.

Agent discovery messages are not required to be authenticated, because no Internet key management protocol was available. Mobile IP secures only registration. Implementations that need privacy or authentication of data packets should use the IP security protocols of RFC 1827 and RFC 1826.
sections.eli5: The home helper only accepts a new address from you if you prove who you are with a secret code, and old messages cannot be replayed to trick it.

sections.title: Evidence for Advancement
sections.content:
At publication, a MIB for Mobile IP existed in RFC 2006. Several implementations were known, from organizations including CMU, FTP Software, IBM, Motorola, Nokia, Sun and Telxon.

FTP Software hosted an interim meeting on October 23-27, 1995 that demonstrated interoperability. Eleven features were tested, among them agent advertisements and solicitations, registration with foreign agents, tunneling in both directions, re-registration after moving or after a foreign agent reboot, and rejection of registrations that failed authentication. Interoperability of at least two independent implementations was shown for all of them, including TCP connections staying open as a node moved away from home and back.

The co-chairs therefore judged that the requirements of RFC 1264 for Proposed Standard were met.
sections.eli5: Several teams built their own versions and showed that they all worked together, even keeping a video-call-style connection alive while moving. That was the proof the idea was ready.
